bullets: His chain is made of ‘cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses wrought in steel’: **symbolism** of greed.
‘I wear the chain I forged in life… I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will’: personal **responsibility**; repetition stresses choice.

‘Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business.’: **repetition** of ‘business’ redefines what a man’s business should be.
Purpose: a **warning**: Scrooge’s fate if he does not change. Gothic horror to grab the reader.
core.p: Scrooge’s former business partner, dead seven years, appears as a ghost bound in chains.

bullets: Its **paradoxical** appearance (child/old man) reflects memory: the past is both young and old.
Light symbolises **truth and memory**; Scrooge’s attempt to extinguish it shows he wants to suppress painful memories.
Method: gentle questions; it lets Scrooge feel rather than lecturing.
Purpose: to awaken **sympathy, memory and regret**.
core.p: A strange figure, ‘like a child: yet not so like a child as like an old man’, with a bright jet of light from its head and holding holly; it also carries a cap like an extinguisher.

bullets: ‘Come in! and know me better, man!’: warm, welcoming imperatives.
His robe leaves his chest bare: openness and generosity.
He sprinkles incense from his torch to bring good humour: blessing the poor most of all.
He ages during the stave, reminding Scrooge that time is short.
Reveals **Ignorance and Want** beneath his robe and throws Scrooge’s words back at him.
Purpose: to show the **present reality** of joy and suffering; social message.
core.p: A ‘jolly Giant’ in a green robe trimmed with fur, surrounded by a feast, carrying a torch shaped like a horn of plenty.

bullets: Resembles the **Grim Reaper**: death and judgement.
It never speaks: silence makes Scrooge (and the reader) interpret what they see.
Shows the consequences of his life: no one mourns him; his goods are stolen.
Purpose: **fear**, the final push to repentance.

callouts.p: The Ghosts move from gentle (Past) to warm and challenging (Present) to terrifying (Yet to Come): Dickens escalates the pressure on Scrooge, and on the reader.

core.h: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
core.p: A silent phantom ‘shrouded in a deep black garment’, showing only one outstretched hand.

model: Marley: warning, chains, ‘Mankind was my business’
Present: abundance, social injustice, Ignorance and Want
Yet to Come: fear, death, consequence
Context: ghost story tradition; Christian afterlife; Dickens’s purpose
exam.q: Explain the importance of the Ghosts elsewhere in the novella. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Explain each ghost’s method and purpose, not just its appearance.

mistakes.r: Marley is separate; he announces the three spirits.
mistakes.w: Marley is one of the three Ghosts.
The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come speaks.

quotes.a: Sin creates its own punishment; personal responsibility.

quotes.a: True business is caring for others.

summary: Marley and the three Ghosts are Dickens’s instruments of change: Marley warns, the Ghost of Christmas Past evokes memory, the Ghost of Christmas Present shows abundance and social injustice, and the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come brings fear of death; know each one’s appearance, method and purpose.

terms.d: A genre using ghosts, darkness and fear.
A contradictory description that reveals a truth.
